definition.raw: A spectral category $\scr{C}$ is \textbf{pointwise cofibrant} if each mapping spectrum $\scr{C}(a, b)$ is cofibrant in the enriching category.
definition.clean: A spectral category scrC is pointwise cofibrant if each mapping spectrum scrC(a, b) is cofibrant in the enriching category.

definition.raw: Let $\scr{C}$ be a spectral category. Then a $\scr{C}$\textbf{-module} is a spectral functor $\scr{C} \to \operatorname{Sp}$.
definition.clean: Let scrC be a spectral category. Then a scrC-module is a spectral functor scrC to Sp.

A (scrC, scrD)-bimodule is a functor scrMcolon scrC^op sma scrD to Sp. That is, scrM is a collection of spectra scrM(c, d) for c in scrC, d in scrD together with maps &scrC(c, c') sma scrM(c', d) to scrM(c, d)\\ &scrM(c, d) sma scrD(d,d') to scrM(c, d') An (scrC, scrD)-bimodule is pointwise cofibrant if scrM(c, d) is cofibrant. A morphism of (scrC, scrD)-bimodules scrM to scrM' is a collection of maps scrM(c, d) to scrM'(c, d) which commute with the appropriate structure.

definition.raw:
Let $\scr{C}$ be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category, and $\scr{Q}$ a $(\scr{C},\scr{C})$-bimodule. The \textbf{topological Hochschild homology of $\scr{C}$ with coefficients in $\scr{Q}$} is the geometric realization of a spectrum whose $n$th simplicial level is
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}; \scr{Q})_n \coloneqq N^{\text{cy}}_n (\scr{C}, \scr{Q}) = \bigvee_{c_0, \dots, c_n} \scr{C}(c_0, c_1) \sma \scr{C}(c_1, c_2) \sma \cdots \sma \scr{C}(c_{n-1}, c_n) \sma \scr{Q}(c_n, c_0)
  \]
  That is, 
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q}) \coloneqq \vert\operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q})_\bullet\vert
  \]
definition.clean: Let scrC be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category, and scrQ a (scrC,scrC)-bimodule. The topological Hochschild homology of scrC with coefficients in scrQ is the geometric realization of a spectrum whose nth simplicial level is \[ THH(scrC; scrQ)_n coloneqq N^cy_n (scrC, scrQ) = bigvee_c_0, dots, c_n scrC(c_0, c_1) sma scrC(c_1, c_2) sma cdots sma scrC(c_n-1, c_n) sma scrQ(c_n, c_0) \] That is, \[ THH(scrC;scrQ) coloneqq vertTHH(scrC;scrQ)_bulletvert \]

definition.raw:
\label{def:base_change}
  Let $F\colon  \scr{A} \to \scr{C}$ and  $G\colon  \scr{B} \to \scr{C}$ be functors between spectral categories. Define an $(\scr{A}, \scr{B})$-bimodule $ \ _F \scr{C}_G$ as follows. For objects $a\in \scr{A}$ and $b \in \scr{B}$
  \[
  \ _F \scr{C}_G (a, b) \coloneqq \scr{C}(F(a), G(b)).  
  \]
 The right action of $\scr{B}$ on $\ _F \scr{C}_G$ is given by the functor $G$:
  \begin{align*}
  \ _F \scr{C}_G(a, b) \sma \scr{B} (b, b') &= \scr{C}(F(a),G(b)) \sma \scr{B} (b, b') \to \scr{C}(F(a), G(b)) \sma \scr{C}(G(b), G(b'))\\ &\to \scr{C} (F(a), G(b')) = \ _F \scr{C}_G (a, b') 
  \end{align*}  The left action of $\scr{A}$ is similar.
definition.clean: Let Fcolon scrA to scrC and Gcolon scrB to scrC be functors between spectral categories. Define an (scrA, scrB)-bimodule \ _F scrC_G as follows. For objects ain scrA and b in scrB \[ \ _F scrC_G (a, b) coloneqq scrC(F(a), G(b)). \] The right action of scrB on \ _F scrC_G is given by the functor G: \ _F scrC_G(a, b) sma scrB (b, b') &= scrC(F(a),G(b)) sma scrB (b, b') to scrC(F(a), G(b)) sma scrC(G(b), G(b'))\\ &to scrC (F(a), G(b')) = \ _F scrC_G (a, b') The left action of scrA is similar.

Let scrB be a bicategory. A shadow functor for scrB consists of functors \[ sh-colon scrB(C,C) to T \] for each object C of scrB and some fixed category T, equipped with a natural isomorphism \[ thetacolon shModot Nxrightarrowcong shNodot M \] for Min scrB(C, D) and Nin scrB(D, C) such that the following diagrams commute whenever they make sense: \[xymatrix sh(Modot N)odot P ar[r]^theta ar[d]_sha & shP odot (Modot N) ar[r]^sha & sh(Podot M) odot N \\ shModot (Nodot P) ar[r]^theta & sh(Nodot P)odot M ar[r]^sha & shNodot (Podot M)ar[u]_theta \] \[xymatrix shModot U_C ar[r]^theta ar[dr]_shr & shU_Codot M ar[d]^shl ar[r]^theta & shModot U_C ar[dl]^shr \\ &shM\]

definition.raw:
We say that a 1-cell $M\in \scr{B}(C,D)$ in a bicategory is \textbf{right dualizable} if there is a 1-cell $N\in \scr{B}(D,C)$, called its \textbf{right dual}, and coevaluation and evaluation 2-cells $\eta\colon U_C \to M\odot N$ and $\epsilon \colon N\odot M\to U_D$ satisfying the triangle identities.
We  say that $(M,N)$ is a \textbf{dual pair}, that $N$ is \textbf{left dualizable}, and that $M$ is its \textbf{left dual}.
definition.clean: We say that a 1-cell Min scrB(C,D) in a bicategory is right dualizable if there is a 1-cell Nin scrB(D,C), called its right dual, and coevaluation and evaluation 2-cells etacolon U_C to Modot N and epsilon colon Nodot Mto U_D satisfying the triangle identities. We say that (M,N) is a dual pair, that N is left dualizable, and that M is its left dual.

definition.raw: define traces of 2-cells associated to dualizable 1-cells.
definition.clean: define traces of 2-cells associated to dualizable 1-cells.

Let scrB be a bicategory with a shadow functor and (M,N) be a dual pair. The trace of a 2-cell fcolon Qodot Mrightarrow Modot P is the composite: \[ shQcong shQodot U_Cxrightarrowshid_Qodoteta shQodot Modot N xrightarrowshfodotid_N shModot Podot N xrightarrowtheta shNodot Modot P xrightarrowshepsilon odot id_P shU_Dodot Pcong shP. \] The trace of a 2-cell gcolon Nodot Qto Podot N is \[ shQcong shU_Codot Qxrightarrowshetaodotid_Q shModot Nodot Q xrightarrowshid_Modot g shModot Podot N xrightarrowtheta shPodot Nodot M xrightarrowshid_P odot epsilon shPodot U_Dcong shP. \]

If Min scrB(C,D) and M is right dualizable, the Euler characteristic (creffig:euler_char) is the trace of the identity 2-cell of M and is a map \[shU_Cto shU_D.\] If N is the right dual of M, chi(M)=chi(N).

A pair of one cells Min scrB(C,D) and Nin scrB(D,C) is a Morita equivalence if (M,N) and (N,M) are dual pairs and the coevaluation and evaluation maps for each dual pair are inverses. That is, if eta_(M,N) and epsilon_(M,N) are the coevaluation and evaluation for (M,N) and eta_(N,M) and epsilon_(N,M) are the coevaluation and evaluation for (N,M) then eta_(N,M)circ epsilon_(M,N)=id_Nodot M & epsilon_(N,M)circ eta_(M,N)=id_U_C \\ eta_(M,N)circ epsilon_(N,M)=id_Modot N& epsilon_(M,N)circ eta_(N,M)=id_U_D

\label{defn:base_change_monoid}
 Let $f\colon  A \to C$ be a morphism in $\mathbf{Mon}(\scr{V})$. Then there is an $(A, C)$-bimodule  $ _f C$, which is $C$ with a left $A$-action given by $f$,  and a $(C, A)$-bimodule $C_f$ which is $C$ with a right $A$-action given by $f$.

Let Fcolon scrA to scrC be a morphism in Cat(scrV), i.e. a functor of categories enriched in scrV. Then there is an (scrA, scrC)-bimodule _F scrC where the left action of scrA is given by scrA(a, a') otimes (_F scrC)(a', c) &= scrA(a, a') otimes scrC(F(a'), c) \\ &to scrC(F(a), F(a')) otimes scrC(F(a'), c) to scrC(F(a), c) = _F scrC(a, c) There is a dual (scrC, scrA)-bimodule that we denote scrC_F.

definition.raw:
A $\sV$-functor $F\colon \sA\to \sC$ 
is a {\bf Morita equivalence} if  $({_F\sC},\sC_F)$ is a Morita equivalence.  
In particular, 
 $F$ is a Morita equivalence if and only if $F$ is full and faithful and the map induced by composition  
\[
 \sC(c,F(-))\odot\sC(F(-),c')\to \sC(c,c')
\] 
is an isomorphism.

definition.raw:
The \textbf{free Moore path space} is defined to be 
  \[
  \scr{P}^M X = \{(\gamma, u) \in \operatorname{Map}([0, \infty), X) \times [0, \infty) : \gamma(t) = \gamma(u) \ t \geq u \}.
      \]
     Here $\operatorname{Map}([0,\infty), X)$ is given the compact open topology. The space $\scr{P}^M X$ comes equipped with two maps $s\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ and $t\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ given by evaluation at $0$ and $u$.
definition.clean: The free Moore path space is defined to be \[ scrP^M X = \(gamma, u) in Map([0, infty), X) times [0, infty) : gamma(t) = gamma(u) \ t geq u \. \] Here Map([0,infty), X) is given the compact open topology. The space scrP^M X comes equipped with two maps scolon scrP^M X to X and tcolon scrP^M X to X given by evaluation at 0 and u.

definition.raw:
Let $X$ be a based space with base $\ast$. Then the \textbf{Moore loop space} is 
  \[
  \Omega^M X = \{(\gamma, u) \in \scr{P}^M X : \gamma(0) = \gamma(u) = \ast\} 
  \]
  that is, it is the pullback
  \[
  \xymatrix{
    \Omega^M X \ar[r]\ar[d] & \scr{P}^MX \ar[d]^{s \times t} \\
    \ast\ar[r]  & X \times X 
  }
  \]
  For work below, it is convenient to denote the ``length'' of the path, $u$, by $|\omega|$.
definition.clean: Let X be a based space with base ast. Then the Moore loop space is \[ Omega^M X = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = gamma(u) = ast\ \] that is, it is the pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^MX ar[d]^s times t \\ astar[r] & X times X \] For work below, it is convenient to denote the ``length'' of the path, u, by |omega|.

The f-twisted Moore loop space is the topological space \[ Omega^M X^f = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = ast, gamma(u) = f(ast)\ \] i.e. it is given as a pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X^f ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^M X ar[d]\\ ast ar[r]^id times f & X times X \] Again, |omega| denotes the length of the path omega.

definition.raw:
The \textbf{$f$-twisted free loop space} is defined to be
  \[
  \scr{L} X^f = \{\gamma \in \scr{P} X : \gamma(0) = f(\gamma(1))\} 
  \]
  That is, $\scr{L} X^f$ arises as the pullback
  \[
  \xymatrix{
    \scr{L} X^f \ar[d]\ar[r] & \scr{P} X \ar[d]^{\operatorname{ev}_0 \times \operatorname{ev}_1}\\
    X \ar[r]^{\operatorname{id} \times f} & X \times X 
  }
  \] 
  Consequently, $\scr{L}^f X$ sits in a fibration sequence
  \[
  \Omega X^f \to \scr{L}^f X \to X 
  \]
definition.clean: The f-twisted free loop space is defined to be \[ scrL X^f = \gamma in scrP X : gamma(0) = f(gamma(1))\ \] That is, scrL X^f arises as the pullback \[ xymatrix scrL X^f ar[d]ar[r] & scrP X ar[d]^ev_0 times ev_1\\ X ar[r]^id times f & X times X \] Consequently, scrL^f X sits in a fibration sequence \[ Omega X^f to scrL^f X to X \]

definition.raw:
$N^{\text{cy}} (\Omega^M X, \Omega^M X^f)$ is the geometric realization of the simplicial space with $n$-simplices
  \[
  N^{\text{cy}}_n (\Omega^M X, \Omega^M X^f) = \underbrace{\Omega^M X \times \cdots \times \Omega^M X}_{n\ \text{times}} \times \Omega^M X^f
  \]
  The face maps $d_i \colon  N^{\text{cy}}_n \to N^{\text{cy}}_{n-1}$ are given by 
  \[
  d_i (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) =
  \begin{cases}
    (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_i \omega_{i+1}, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) & i < n \\
    (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1} \omega) & i = n \\
    (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega f(\omega_0)) & i = n+1
  \end{cases}
  \]
  The degeneracies $s_j \colon  N^{cy}_{n} \to N^{\text{cy}}_{n+1}$ are given by the insertion of trivial paths:
  \[
    s_j (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) = (\cdots, \omega_{j}, \ast, \omega_{j+1}, \dots)
  \]
definition.clean: N^cy (Omega^M X, Omega^M X^f) is the geometric realization of the simplicial space with n-simplices \[ N^cy_n (Omega^M X, Omega^M X^f) = underbraceOmega^M X times cdots times Omega^M X_n\ times times Omega^M X^f \] The face maps d_i colon N^cy_n to N^cy_n-1 are given by \[ d_i (omega_0, dots, omega_n-1, omega) = (omega_0, dots, omega_i omega_i+1, dots, omega_n-1, omega) & i < n \\ (omega_0, dots, omega_n-1 omega) & i = n \\ (omega_1, dots, omega_n-1, omega f(omega_0)) & i = n+1 \] The degeneracies s_j colon N^cy_n to N^cy_n+1 are given by the insertion of trivial paths: \[ s_j (omega_0, dots, omega_n-1, omega) = (cdots, omega_j, ast, omega_j+1, dots) \]

definition.raw:
The space $(\Omega X^f)^{\Delta^n}$ is defined to be 
  \[
  (\Omega X^f )^{\Delta^n} = \left\{\gamma \in \operatorname{Map}(\Delta^n, \scr{P} X) \biggr| \begin{matrix}\gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n} (0) = \ast, \gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n}(1) = f(\ast)\\ \text{for all}\ (u_0, \dots, u_n) \in \Delta^n \end{matrix}\right\}
  \]
  The cosimplicial structure on $\Delta^\bullet$ induces a simplicial structure on $(\Omega X^f)^{\Delta^\bullet}$.  The face maps are given by restriction:
  \[
  d_i (\gamma)(t, u_0, \dots, u_n) = \gamma(t, u_0, \dots,u_i, 0, u_{i+1}, \dots, u_n) 
 \]
  where $t$ is the path coordinate and the degeneracy maps are given by addition of coordinates:
  \[
  s_i (\gamma)(t, u_0, \dots, u_n) = \gamma(t, u_0, \dots, u_i + u_{i+1}, \dots, u_n) 
  \]
definition.clean: The space (Omega X^f)^Delta^n is defined to be \[ (Omega X^f )^Delta^n = left\gamma in Map(Delta^n, scrP X) biggr| gamma_u_0, dots, u_n (0) = ast, gamma_u_0, dots, u_n(1) = f(ast)\\ for all\ (u_0, dots, u_n) in Delta^n right\ \] The cosimplicial structure on Delta^bullet induces a simplicial structure on (Omega X^f)^Delta^bullet. The face maps are given by restriction: \[ d_i (gamma)(t, u_0, dots, u_n) = gamma(t, u_0, dots,u_i, 0, u_i+1, dots, u_n) \] where t is the path coordinate and the degeneracy maps are given by addition of coordinates: \[ s_i (gamma)(t, u_0, dots, u_n) = gamma(t, u_0, dots, u_i + u_i+1, dots, u_n) \]

definition.raw:
The topological space $(\scr{L} X^f)^{\Delta^n}$ is defined to be

  (\scr{L} X^f)^{\Delta^n} = \left\{\gamma \in \operatorname{Map}(\Delta^n, \scr{P} X)\biggr|\begin{matrix} \gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n} (0) = f (\gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n} (1)) \\ \text{for all}\ (u_0, \dots, u_n) \in \Delta^n \end{matrix}\right\}

Again, the cosimplicial structure on $\Delta^\bullet$ induces a simplicial structure on $(\scr{L} X^f)^{\Delta^\bullet}$. The face and degeneracy maps are as above.

theorem.raw:
\label{thm:lm_generalization}
  Let $X$ be a topological space homotopy equivalent to a finite CW-complex. The Reidemeister trace is naturally equivalent to the $\operatorname{THH}$ transfer
  \[
    \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_S) \to  \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X})\to  \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X}; F).
  \]
theorem.clean: Let X be a topological space homotopy equivalent to a finite CW-complex. The Reidemeister trace is naturally equivalent to the THH transfer \[ THH(Mod^c_S) to THH(Mod^c_Sigma^infty_+ Omega X)to THH(Mod^c_Sigma^infty_+ Omega X; F). \]

theorem.raw:
\label{thm:what_happens_on_pi}
 The image of $[f] \in \pi_0 \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$ under the Morita invariance isomorphism 
 \[
   \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A) \simeq \operatorname{THH}(A)
  \]
  is the bicategorical trace of $f$. In particular, for a module $M \in \operatorname{Mod}^c_A$, the image of $[\operatorname{id}_M]$ is $\chi(M)$.

theorem.raw:

proof.raw:
The main property of shadows is that for $(\scr{C}, \scr{D})$-bimodule $\scr{M}$ and a $(\scr{D}, \scr{C})$-bimodule $\scr{N}$, there is an isomorphism
  \[
  \theta \colon  \sh{\scr{M} \odot \scr{N}}  \to \sh{\scr{N} \odot \scr{M}}. 
  \]
  Unpacking this into the usual notation, this is equivalent to the demand that there is an isomorphism 
  \[
  \theta\colon  \operatorname{THH} (\scr{C}, B(\scr{M}, \scr{D}, \scr{N})) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{D}, B(\scr{N}, \scr{C}, \scr{M})) 
  \]
  However, this is the classical Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen argument \cite[Prop.~6.2]{blumberg_mandell} --- in this case, there is an isomorphism of underlying point-set spectra.

  The commutativity of the rest of the diagrams follow from essentially the same argument.

A good example to keep in mind is the following. Let $A$ be a commutative ring spectrum,  $P$ be an $A$-module, and let $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ denote the category of compact $A$-modules. example.raw:
For rings $C$ and $D$, an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right $D$-module.  
A choice of dual is the $(D,C)$-bimodule of right $D$-module homomorphisms $\Hom_D(M,D)$.  Note that $\Hom_D(M,D)$ is regarded as a $(D,C)$-bimodule using the left $C$-module structure on $M$ and left $D$-module structure on $D$. 

The coevaluation map is the composite  
\[
  C\to \Hom_D(M,M)\xleftarrow{\sim} M\otimes_D\Hom_D(M,D)
\] 
where
the second map is an isomorphism since $M$ is  finitely generated and projective as an $D$ module. 
The evaluation map for this dual pair is the  evaluation map 
\[
  \Hom_D(M,D)\otimes_C M\to D.
\]

Dually, $M$ is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left $C$-module.
example.clean: For rings C and D, an (C,D)-bimodule M is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right D-module. A choice of dual is the (D,C)-bimodule of right D-module homomorphisms Hom_D(M,D). Note that Hom_D(M,D) is regarded as a (D,C)-bimodule using the left C-module structure on M and left D-module structure on D. The coevaluation map is the composite \[ Cto Hom_D(M,M)xleftarrowsim Motimes_DHom_D(M,D) \] where the second map is an isomorphism since M is finitely generated and projective as an D module. The evaluation map for this dual pair is the evaluation map \[ Hom_D(M,D)otimes_C Mto D. \] Dually, M is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left C-module.

example.raw:
Costenoble-Waner duality \cite[Chapter~18]{maysig:pht} is a special case of the duality theory above and generalizes Spanier-Whitehead and Atiyah duality.  

The parameterized stable homotopy category $\operatorname{Ex}$ of \cite{maysig:pht} has a fiberwise suspension spectrum functor  from the bicategory of fibered spaces (without sections).  If we regard a closed smooth manifold $X$, or compact ENR, as a space over $\ast\times X$  its fiberwise suspension spectrum is dualizable with dual the desuspension of the fiberwise one point compactification of the normal bundle \cite[18.5.1]{maysig:pht}.

In the bicategory of rings, bimodules, and homomorphisms, a Morita equivalence is a $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ and a $(D,C)$-bimodule $N$ so that  $(M,N)$ and $(N,M)$ are dual pairs and, using the coevaluation and evaluation from these dual pairs, 
 \[
  M\otimes_DN\cong C\qquad\text{and} \qquad N\otimes_CM\cong D.
 \]
This is the familiar notion of Morita equivalence for rings and implies the  functor 
\[
 N\otimes_C- \colon \Mod_C\to \Mod_D
\] 
is equivalence of the category of (left) modules over $C$ and the category of (left) modules over $D$. 

The most familiar example of Morita equivalence is that the ring of $n$-by-$n$ matrices with elements in $C$ is Morita equivalent to $C$ for any $n > 0$.

Let $A$ be a ring spectrum,  $Q$ be an $(A,A)$-bimodule, and

an  $(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A, \operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$-bimodule and the inclusion 
\[
  E_A\colon  \End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A) \to \operatorname{Mod}^c_A
\] 
defines a $(\End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A),\End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A))$-bimodule  $_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}$.

gives an isomorphism $\sh{_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}} \to \sh{(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}}$. We also have identifications
  \begin{align*}

We present two examples of these types of restriction-transfer identities
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $X$ be a path-connected space of  the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex. If we let $A=S$ and $C=\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X$, then $A$ is compact as a $C$-module.  The composite 
  \[
  S \simeq \operatorname{THH} (S) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}  \operatorname{THH} (\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{THH} (S) \simeq S 
  \]
is $\chi(X)$, regarded as an element of $\pi_0(S)$.
\item Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ where $[G:H] < \infty$.  Then the base change object associated to the inclusion of the group ring $A = \mathbb{Z}[H]$ into $C = \mathbb{Z}[G]$ is dualizable. The shadow is $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G])$ and 
  \[
  \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H],\mathbb{Z}[H]) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}   \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G],\mathbb{Z}[G]) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H], \mathbb{Z}[H]) 
  \]
  is multiplication by $[G:H]$. This has an interpretation in terms of the character theory of group representations, since $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G]) \cong \mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ where $C_G$ denotes the conjugacy classes of $G$. Since maps from $\mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ are exactly class functions, this is the same $[G:H]$ that appears in the classical induction-restriction maps in character theory for representations of finite groups.
\end{itemize}

\label{ex_ab_group_base_change}
If $\scr{V}$ is the category of abelian groups and categories $\scr{C}$ and $\scr{D}$ each have  a single object, $\scr{C}$ is a ring $C$,  $\scr{D}$ is a ring $D$.  An $(\scr{C}, \scr{D}$)-bimodule $\scr{M}$ is an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$.  
If $i\colon \mathbb{Z}\to C$ is the map that picks out the monoidal unit, 
\[\rbm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iC}\to{_iC}\] is the ring multiplication in $C$ and 
\[\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iM}\to {_iM} \] is the module structure map.  

If $f\colon A\to C$ is a ring homomorphism, and $M$ is an $(C,D)$-bimodule 
\[\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{A}{A}{_fM}\colon _iA_i\otimes{ _i({_fM})}\to {_i({_fM})} \]

  Let $\scr{V}$ be the category of abelian groups. For a ring $C$ and a finitely generated projective $C$-module $P$, 
an endomorphism $f\colon P \to P$ is represented by a map of abelian groups $\mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{[f]} \Hom(P, P)$, i.e. a map of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules. Despite the fact that $\Hom(P, P)$ has the structure of a monoid, the map is \textit{not} a map of monoids.

We consider the case when $n = 2$ for the map $B$ above, which is enough to capture the issues. We define
  \[
  \widetilde{\omega} = \omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)
  \]
  and  a family of paths parameterized by the 2-simplex \[\Delta^2 = \{(u_0, u_1, u_2) : u_0 + u_1 + u_2 = 1\}.\] 
We think of this simplex as interpolating between three extremes: the cases when each of $u_0, u_1$ and $u_2$ are 1. We'd like the extreme cases to be
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $u_2 = 1$ --- the path $\omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega$
  \item $u_1 = 1$ --- the path $\omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0)$
  \item $u_0 = 1$ --- the path $\omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)$. 
  \end{itemize}
  We would also like that if the path starts at $x$, the endpoint is $f(x)$. Consider the path 
  \begin{align*}
    \widetilde{\omega} (t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1| + |\omega|) + u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|))
  \end{align*}
  We can check that when $u_2 = 1$ then $u_0, u_1 = 0$ and the above gives $\widetilde{\omega}(t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|+|\omega|))$ which is exactly $\omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega$. When $u_1 = 1$, then the above is $\widetilde{\omega}(t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + |\omega_0|)$, which is the path $\omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0)$. Finally, when $u_0 = 1$ we get the path $\omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)$.

  We also note that for any choice of $u_0, u_1$, 
  \begin{align*}
    &\widetilde{\omega}(u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|)\\
    &= \widetilde{\omega} (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1| + |\omega| + u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|))
  \end{align*}
  essentially by definition, so that each path parameterized by $u_0, u_1, u_2$ is in $\scr{L} X^f$.

\begin{defn}
  Let $\scr{C}$ be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category, and $\scr{Q}$ a $(\scr{C},\scr{C})$-bimodule. The \textbf{topological Hochschild homology of $\scr{C}$ with coefficients in $\scr{Q}$} is the geometric realization of a spectrum whose $n$th simplicial level is
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}; \scr{Q})_n \coloneqq N^{\text{cy}}_n (\scr{C}, \scr{Q}) = \bigvee_{c_0, \dots, c_n} \scr{C}(c_0, c_1) \sma \scr{C}(c_1, c_2) \sma \cdots \sma \scr{C}(c_{n-1}, c_n) \sma \scr{Q}(c_n, c_0)
  \]
  That is, 
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q}) \coloneqq \vert\operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q})_\bullet\vert
  \]
\end{defn}

\begin{defn}
  The \textbf{free Moore path space} is defined to be 
  \[
  \scr{P}^M X = \{(\gamma, u) \in \operatorname{Map}([0, \infty), X) \times [0, \infty) : \gamma(t) = \gamma(u) \ t \geq u \}.
      \]
     Here $\operatorname{Map}([0,\infty), X)$ is given the compact open topology. The space $\scr{P}^M X$ comes equipped with two maps $s\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ and $t\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ given by evaluation at $0$ and $u$. 
\end{defn}

The space scrP^M X comes equipped with two maps scolon scrP^M X to X and tcolon scrP^M X to X given by evaluation at 0 and u.

Let X be a based space with base ast. Then the Moore loop space is \[ Omega^M X = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = gamma(u) = ast\ \] that is, it is the pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^MX ar[d]^s times t \\ astar[r] & X times X \] For work below, it is convenient to denote the ``length'' of the path, u, by |omega|.

The f-twisted Moore loop space is the topological space \[ Omega^M X^f = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = ast, gamma(u) = f(ast)\ \] i.e. it is given as a pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X^f ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^M X ar[d]\\ ast ar[r]^id times f & X times X \] Again, |omega| denotes the length of the path omega.

  The face maps $d_i \colon  N^{\text{cy}}_n \to N^{\text{cy}}_{n-1}$ are given by 
  \[
  d_i (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) =
  \begin{cases}
    (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_i \omega_{i+1}, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) & i < n \\
    (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1} \omega) & i = n \\
    (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega f(\omega_0)) & i = n+1
  \end{cases}
  \]
  The degeneracies $s_j \colon  N^{cy}_{n} \to N^{\text{cy}}_{n+1}$ are given by the insertion of trivial paths:
  \[
    s_j (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}, \omega) = (\cdots, \omega_{j}, \ast, \omega_{j+1}, \dots)
  \]
\end{defn}

  The space $(\Omega X^f)^{\Delta^n}$ is defined to be 
  \[
  (\Omega X^f )^{\Delta^n} = \left\{\gamma \in \operatorname{Map}(\Delta^n, \scr{P} X) \biggr| \begin{matrix}\gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n} (0) = \ast, \gamma_{u_0, \dots, u_n}(1) = f(\ast)\\ \text{for all}\ (u_0, \dots, u_n) \in \Delta^n \end{matrix}\right\}
  \]
  The cosimplicial structure on $\Delta^\bullet$ induces a simplicial structure on $(\Omega X^f)^{\Delta^\bullet}$.  The face maps are given by restriction:

 \]

  \[
  s_i (\gamma)(t, u_0, \dots, u_n) = \gamma(t, u_0, \dots, u_i + u_{i+1}, \dots, u_n) 
  \]
\end{defn}

\begin{defn}
  Let $\scr{C}$ be a pointwise cofibrant spectral category, and $\scr{Q}$ a $(\scr{C},\scr{C})$-bimodule. The \textbf{topological Hochschild homology of $\scr{C}$ with coefficients in $\scr{Q}$} is the geometric realization of a spectrum whose $n$th simplicial level is
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}; \scr{Q})_n \coloneqq N^{\text{cy}}_n (\scr{C}, \scr{Q}) = \bigvee_{c_0, \dots, c_n} \scr{C}(c_0, c_1) \sma \scr{C}(c_1, c_2) \sma \cdots \sma \scr{C}(c_{n-1}, c_n) \sma \scr{Q}(c_n, c_0)
  \]
  That is, 
  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q}) \coloneqq \vert\operatorname{THH}(\scr{C};\scr{Q})_\bullet\vert
  \]
\end{defn}

\begin{defn}
  The \textbf{free Moore path space} is defined to be 
  \[
  \scr{P}^M X = \{(\gamma, u) \in \operatorname{Map}([0, \infty), X) \times [0, \infty) : \gamma(t) = \gamma(u) \ t \geq u \}.
      \]
     Here $\operatorname{Map}([0,\infty), X)$ is given the compact open topology. The space $\scr{P}^M X$ comes equipped with two maps $s\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ and $t\colon  \scr{P}^M X \to X$ given by evaluation at $0$ and $u$. 
\end{defn}

The space scrP^M X comes equipped with two maps scolon scrP^M X to X and tcolon scrP^M X to X given by evaluation at 0 and u.

Let X be a based space with base ast. Then the Moore loop space is \[ Omega^M X = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = gamma(u) = ast\ \] that is, it is the pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^MX ar[d]^s times t \\ astar[r] & X times X \] For work below, it is convenient to denote the ``length'' of the path, u, by |omega|.

The f-twisted Moore loop space is the topological space \[ Omega^M X^f = \(gamma, u) in scrP^M X : gamma(0) = ast, gamma(u) = f(ast)\ \] i.e. it is given as a pullback \[ xymatrix Omega^M X^f ar[r]ar[d] & scrP^M X ar[d]\\ ast ar[r]^id times f & X times X \] Again, |omega| denotes the length of the path omega.

\begin{defn}
  The \textbf{$f$-twisted free loop space} is defined to be
  \[
  \scr{L} X^f = \{\gamma \in \scr{P} X : \gamma(0) = f(\gamma(1))\} 
  \]
  That is, $\scr{L} X^f$ arises as the pullback
  \[
  \xymatrix{
    \scr{L} X^f \ar[d]\ar[r] & \scr{P} X \ar[d]^{\operatorname{ev}_0 \times \operatorname{ev}_1}\\
    X \ar[r]^{\operatorname{id} \times f} & X \times X 
  }
  \] 
  Consequently, $\scr{L}^f X$ sits in a fibration sequence
  \[
  \Omega X^f \to \scr{L}^f X \to X

Outline
In \cref{sect:thh_spectral} we establish some results about the bicategory of spectral categories, and how $\operatorname{THH}$ behaves on these. We prove that $\operatorname{THH}$ is a shadow in the sense of \cite{p:thesis}. In \cref{sect:duality_and_trace} we define traces and Euler characteristics in bicategories. In the bicategorical context, the Euler characteristic is an invariant of 1-cells, and we establish a number of results about the composition of these characteristics. 

\cref{morita_equivalence} and \cref{sect:euler_char} are devoted to the properties of traces and Euler characteristics under Morita invariance. These are the technical core of the paper, and every result needed to address the main example is treated in great generality in these sections. \cref{morita_equivalence} addresses how traces behave with respect to Morita invariance, while \cref{sect:euler_char} discusses how bicategorical Euler characteristics behave under certain base change maps. 

Having related shadows and $\operatorname{THH}$, in \cref{sect:transfer} we relate the transfer in $\operatorname{THH}$ to the Reidemeister trace. This is achieved by observing that transfers in $\operatorname{THH}$ are nothing more than an example of base change. The results from \cref{morita_equivalence} and \cref{sect:euler_char} then allow us to very explicitly identify certain transfers.

In \cref{sect:cyclotomic} we show that the ``inclusion of objects'' map on $\operatorname{THH}$ is exactly computed by the bicategorical trace, finally relating the two notions of trace that arise in the literature. 

A crucial, but lengthy, computation is relegated to the appendix.

In this statement $\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$ is the category of compact $A$ modules. The object $\operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A; F)$ is a twisted variant of $\operatorname{THH}$ (\cref{right_twisted}). 

The equivalence referenced in \cref{thm:lm_generalization} is induced by Morita equivalences, which are maps
\[
 \operatorname{THH}(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A).
\]
In this direction the map is not hard to define, but the homotopy inverse is far less obvious.  It would be desirable to know the inverse. We give a reasonably description of the inverse, and give a very explicit description on $\pi_0$.

For a ring spectrum $A$, an endomorphism $f\colon M \to M$ of a compact $A$-module spectrum determines a map 
$S\to \operatorname{End}(M) $.  Composing with the inclusion of the zero skeleton defines a map 
\[
  S\to \operatorname{End}(M) \to \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A) 
\]
and so an element $[f] \in \pi_0 \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$. This sets up the second main theorem of this paper.

 \]
is a weak equivalence.  Thus, for instance, if $Q\scr{P} \to \scr{P}$ is a cofibrant replacement of $\scr{P}$, $\operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}, Q\scr{P}) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}, \scr{P})$ is a weak equivalence.

These propositions imply that can move  between models and replace bimodules by weakly equivalent ones at will. Given this, we work on the level of homotopy categories.



\begin{defn}
  The bicategory of small spectral categories is the bicategory whose objects are pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories, and whose morphism categories are 
\[
 \operatorname{Ho}\left(\operatorname{Mod}_{(\scr{C}, \scr{D})}\right)
\]
 for pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories $\scr{C}$ and $\scr{D}$.
\end{defn}

\begin{rmk} 
  The composition of 1-cells is defined as follows. Let $\scr{M}$ be an $(\scr{C}, \scr{D})$-bimodule and $\scr{N}$ an $(\scr{D},\scr{E})$-bimodule. Then we may form an $(\scr{C}, \scr{E})$-bimodule $\scr{M} \odot \scr{N}$
  \begin{align*}
    (\scr{M} \odot \scr{N})(c,e) &\coloneqq \scr{M}(c,-) \sma^{\mathbf{L}}_{\scr{D}} \scr{N}(-,e)\\
    &\coloneqq B(\scr{M}(c,-), \scr{D}, \scr{N}(-,e))
  \end{align*}
  where $B(-,-,-)$ denotes the two-sided bar construction. 
  
  This descends to
  \[
  \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{C}, \scr{D})}\right) \times \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{D}, \scr{E})}\right) \to \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{C}, \scr{E})}\right)
  \]
  Checking that this is associative is straightforward but tedious. One explicitly writes out the bar construction and cofibrantly replaces as needed.  The composition of 2-cells is the composition of natural transformations. 
\end{rmk} 

As a cyclic bar construction, $\operatorname{THH}$ has cyclic invariance built into it.  This cyclic invariance is also present in Hochschild homology and is an essential part of  the Hattori-Stallings  trace 
\[
K_0(A)\to HH_0(A).
\] 
There is a general categorical setup due to the second named author \cite{p:thesis} that encodes exactly the kind of properties that $\operatorname{THH}$ enjoys as a functor of spectral categories. 


\begin{defn}[\cite{p:thesis}]\label{def:shadow}
  Let $\scr{B}$ be a bicategory.  A \textbf{shadow functor} for $\scr{B}$
  consists of functors
  \[
   \sh{-}\colon  \scr{B}(C,C) \to \mathbf{T}

  \[

  \]
  for $M\in \scr{B}(C, D)$ and $N\in \scr{B}(D, C)$ such that the following

  \[\xymatrix{

Thus, for instance, if QscrP to scrP is a cofibrant replacement of scrP, THH(scrC, QscrP) to THH(scrC, scrP) is a weak equivalence. These propositions imply that can move between models and replace bimodules by weakly equivalent ones at will. Given this, we work on the level of homotopy categories. The bicategory of small spectral categories is the bicategory whose objects are pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories, and whose morphism categories are \[ Holeft(Mod_(scrC, scrD)right) \] for pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories scrC and scrD. The composition of 1-cells is defined as follows. Let scrM be an (scrC, scrD)-bimodule and scrN an (scrD,scrE)-bimodule. Then we may form an (scrC, scrE)-bimodule scrM odot scrN (scrM odot scrN)(c,e) &coloneqq scrM(c,-) sma^L_scrD scrN(-,e)\\ &coloneqq B(scrM(c,-), scrD, scrN(-,e)) where B(-,-,-) denotes the two-sided bar construction. This descends to \[ Holeft(Mod_(scrC, scrD)right) times Holeft(Mod_(scrD, scrE)right) to Holeft(Mod_(scrC, scrE)right) \] Checking that this is associative is straightforward but tedious. One explicitly writes out the bar construction and cofibrantly replaces as needed. The composition of 2-cells is the composition of natural transformations. As a cyclic bar construction, THH has cyclic invariance built into it. This cyclic invariance is also present in Hochschild homology and is an essential part of the Hattori-Stallings trace \[ K_0(A)to HH_0(A). \] There is a general categorical setup due to the second named author that encodes exactly the kind of properties that THH enjoys as a functor of spectral categories. A shadow functor for scrB consists of functors \[ sh-colon scrB(C,C) to T \] for each object C of scrB and some fixed category T, equipped with a natural isomorphism \[ thetacolon shModot Nxrightarrowcong shNodot M \] for Min scrB(C, D) and Nin scrB(D, C) such that the following diagrams commute whenever they make sense: \[xymatrix sh(Modot N)odot P ar[r]^theta ar[d]_sha & shP odot (Modot N) ar[r]^sha & sh(Podot M) odot N \\ shModot (Nodot P) ar[r]^theta & sh(Nodot P)odot M ar[r]^sha & shNodot (Podot M)ar[u]_theta \] \[xymatrix shModot U_C ar[r]^theta ar[dr]_shr & shU_Codot M ar[d]^shl ar[r]^theta & shModot U_C ar[dl]^shr \\ &shM\] Note that if sh- is a shadow functor on scrB, then the composite \[xymatrix shModot N ar[r]^theta & shNodot M ar[r]^theta & shModot N \] is the identity .

\begin{proof}


  
  The main property of shadows is that for $(\scr{C}, \scr{D})$-bimodule $\scr{M}$ and a $(\scr{D}, \scr{C})$-bimodule $\scr{N}$, there is an isomorphism
  \[
  \theta \colon  \sh{\scr{M} \odot \scr{N}}  \to \sh{\scr{N} \odot \scr{M}}. 
  \]
  Unpacking this into the usual notation, this is equivalent to the demand that there is an isomorphism 
  \[
  \theta\colon  \operatorname{THH} (\scr{C}, B(\scr{M}, \scr{D}, \scr{N})) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{D}, B(\scr{N}, \scr{C}, \scr{M})) 
  \]
  However, this is the classical Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen argument \cite[Prop.~6.2]{blumberg_mandell} --- in this case, there is an isomorphism of underlying point-set spectra.

  The commutativity of the rest of the diagrams follow from essentially the same argument. 
\end{proof}

\[\rbm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iC}\to{_iC}\] is the ring multiplication in $C$ and 
\[\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iM}\to {_iM} \] is the module structure map.  

If $f\colon A\to C$ is a ring homomorphism, and $M$ is an $(C,D)$-bimodule

\[M\cong \bZ\otimes {_iM}\xrightarrow{\alpha\otimes \id} {_iC_i}\otimes {_iM} \xrightarrow{\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}} {_iM}\] is given by $n\mapsto \alpha(1)n$.

    &\coloneqq B(\scr{M}(c,-), \scr{D}, \scr{N}(-,e))
  \end{align*}
  where $B(-,-,-)$ denotes the two-sided bar construction. 
  
  This descends to
  \[
  \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{C}, \scr{D})}\right) \times \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{D}, \scr{E})}\right) \to \operatorname{Ho}\left(\Mod_{(\scr{C}, \scr{E})}\right)
  \]
  Checking that this is associative is straightforward but tedious. One explicitly writes out the bar construction and cofibrantly replaces as needed.  The composition of 2-cells is the composition of natural transformations. 
\end{rmk} 

As a cyclic bar construction, $\operatorname{THH}$ has cyclic invariance built into it.  This cyclic invariance is also present in Hochschild homology and is an essential part of  the Hattori-Stallings  trace 
\[
K_0(A)\to HH_0(A).
\] 
There is a general categorical setup due to the second named author \cite{p:thesis} that encodes exactly the kind of properties that $\operatorname{THH}$ enjoys as a functor of spectral categories. 


\begin{defn}[\cite{p:thesis}]\label{def:shadow}
  Let $\scr{B}$ be a bicategory.  A \textbf{shadow functor} for $\scr{B}$
  consists of functors
  \[
   \sh{-}\colon  \scr{B}(C,C) \to \mathbf{T}
  \]
  for each object $C$ of $\scr{B}$ and some fixed category $\mathbf{T}$, equipped
  with a natural isomorphism
  \[
   \theta\colon \sh{M\odot N}\xrightarrow{\cong} \sh{N\odot M}
  \]
  for $M\in \scr{B}(C, D)$ and $N\in \scr{B}(D, C)$ such that the following
  diagrams commute whenever they make sense:
  \[\xymatrix{
    \sh{(M\odot N)\odot P} \ar[r]^\theta \ar[d]_{\sh{a}} &
    \sh{P \odot (M\odot N)} \ar[r]^{\sh{a}} &
    \sh{(P\odot M) \odot N}
    \\
    \sh{M\odot (N\odot P)} \ar[r]^\theta 
    & \sh{(N\odot P)\odot M} \ar[r]^{\sh{a}} 
   & \sh{N\odot (P\odot M)}\ar[u]_\theta 
  }\]
  \[\xymatrix{
    \sh{M\odot U_C} \ar[r]^\theta \ar[dr]_{\sh{r}} &
    \sh{U_C\odot M} \ar[d]^{\sh{l}} \ar[r]^\theta &
    \sh{M\odot U_C} \ar[dl]^{\sh{r}}
    \\
    &\sh{M}}\]
\end{defn}

Note that   if $\sh{-}$ is a shadow functor on $\scr{B}$, then the composite
  \[\xymatrix{
    \sh{M\odot N} \ar[r]^\theta &
    \sh{N\odot M} \ar[r]^\theta &
    \sh{M\odot N}
   }\]
  is the identity \cite[Prop.~4.3]{ps:bicat}.

\begin{proof}


  
  The main property of shadows is that for $(\scr{C}, \scr{D})$-bimodule $\scr{M}$ and a $(\scr{D}, \scr{C})$-bimodule $\scr{N}$, there is an isomorphism
  \[
  \theta \colon  \sh{\scr{M} \odot \scr{N}}  \to \sh{\scr{N} \odot \scr{M}}. 
  \]
  Unpacking this into the usual notation, this is equivalent to the demand that there is an isomorphism 
  \[
  \theta\colon  \operatorname{THH} (\scr{C}, B(\scr{M}, \scr{D}, \scr{N})) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{D}, B(\scr{N}, \scr{C}, \scr{M})) 
  \]
  However, this is the classical Dennis-Morita-Waldhausen argument \cite[Prop.~6.2]{blumberg_mandell} --- in this case, there is an isomorphism of underlying point-set spectra.

  The commutativity of the rest of the diagrams follow from essentially the same argument. 
\end{proof}

Let $\scr{V} = \mathbf{Sp}$. Then $\scr{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\scr{V}))$ is the bicategory of spectral categories. Because of the homotopical issues outlined above we work in the full subcategory of pointwise cofibrant small spectral categories. In general, if $\scr{V}$ and $\mathbf{Cat}(\scr{V})$ have some kind of homotopical structure, we understand $\scr{B}(\mathbf{Cat}(\scr{V}))$ to be modified in order to give the homotopically correct definitions.

While we will not use them as a formal proof, some of the results in the next sections have illuminating graphical descriptions as pasting diagrams.  

In our pasting diagrams vertices represent 0-cells, edges represent 1-cells, and colored regions represent 2-cells.  Since we will need to eventually make circular diagrams (\cref{fig:pasting_trace}), we do not identify 0-cells when they are the same.  Instead we rely on the convention that vertices in consecutive layers that align should be regarded as the same.
We suppress unit isomorphisms and many unit 1-cells.  Pale gray regions are identity 2-cells.

See \cref{fig;dual_pairs} for pasting diagrams for a dual pair.

For rings $C$ and $D$, an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right $D$-module.  
A choice of dual is the $(D,C)$-bimodule of right $D$-module homomorphisms $\Hom_D(M,D)$.  Note that $\Hom_D(M,D)$ is regarded as a $(D,C)$-bimodule using the left $C$-module structure on $M$ and left $D$-module structure on $D$. 

The coevaluation map is the composite  
\[
  C\to \Hom_D(M,M)\xleftarrow{\sim} M\otimes_D\Hom_D(M,D)
\] 
where
the second map is an isomorphism since $M$ is  finitely generated and projective as an $D$ module. 
The evaluation map for this dual pair is the  evaluation map 
\[
  \Hom_D(M,D)\otimes_C M\to D.
\]

Dually, $M$ is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left $C$-module.
items.clean: For rings C and D, an (C,D)-bimodule M is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right D-module. A choice of dual is the (D,C)-bimodule of right D-module homomorphisms Hom_D(M,D). Note that Hom_D(M,D) is regarded as a (D,C)-bimodule using the left C-module structure on M and left D-module structure on D. The coevaluation map is the composite \[ Cto Hom_D(M,M)xleftarrowsim Motimes_DHom_D(M,D) \] where the second map is an isomorphism since M is finitely generated and projective as an D module. The evaluation map for this dual pair is the evaluation map \[ Hom_D(M,D)otimes_C Mto D. \] Dually, M is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left C-module.

Costenoble-Waner duality \cite[Chapter~18]{maysig:pht} is a special case of the duality theory above and generalizes Spanier-Whitehead and Atiyah duality.  

The parameterized stable homotopy category $\operatorname{Ex}$ of \cite{maysig:pht} has a fiberwise suspension spectrum functor  from the bicategory of fibered spaces (without sections).  If we regard a closed smooth manifold $X$, or compact ENR, as a space over $\ast\times X$  its fiberwise suspension spectrum is dualizable with dual the desuspension of the fiberwise one point compactification of the normal bundle \cite[18.5.1]{maysig:pht}.

In \cite{dold_puppe}, there is a particularly elegant proof of the Lefschetz fixed point theorem that  relies on the observations that the fixed point index \cite{dold_idx} is the trace in the stable homotopy category, the Lefschetz number is the trace in the homotopy category of chain complexes, 
and the symmetric monoidal trace is functorial: that is 
\[
  F(\tr(f))=\tr(F(f)).
\]
The Reidemeister trace, in its many variants, is an example of the bicategorical trace \cite{p:thesis}.  Since these are bicategorical traces, the identification of the varied forms of the Reidemeister trace 
is a consequence of the functoriality of the bicategorical trace.

In the bicategory of rings, bimodules, and homomorphisms, a Morita equivalence is a $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ and a $(D,C)$-bimodule $N$ so that  $(M,N)$ and $(N,M)$ are dual pairs and, using the coevaluation and evaluation from these dual pairs, 
 \[
  M\otimes_DN\cong C\qquad\text{and} \qquad N\otimes_CM\cong D.
 \]
This is the familiar notion of Morita equivalence for rings and implies the  functor 
\[
 N\otimes_C- \colon \Mod_C\to \Mod_D
\] 
is equivalence of the category of (left) modules over $C$ and the category of (left) modules over $D$. 

The most familiar example of Morita equivalence is that the ring of $n$-by-$n$ matrices with elements in $C$ is Morita equivalent to $C$ for any $n > 0$.

Let scrB(Cat(Sp)) be the bicategory of spectral categories (with the proper homotopy theoretic considerations, see crefbcat_example) . Let A be a ring spectrum. There are two spectral categories naturally associated with A item The spectral category Mod^c_A. item The one object spectral category whose hom spectrum is A. We denote this category End_ Mod^c_A(A) since it is the full subcategory of Mod^c_A with the single object A. There is an inclusion functor \[ E_Acolon End_ Mod^c_A(A) to Mod^c_A \] and so we can construct a 1-cell (i.e. a spectral bimodule) _E_A (Mod^c_A). There is similarly a spectral bimodule (Mod^c_A)_E_A. These two bimodules are a Morita equivalence. Applying crefcor:base_change_morita_isos with the substitutions c|c|c scrA & scrC & F\\hline End_Mod^c_A (A) & Mod^c_A & E_A the map THH(A) cong THHleft(End_Mod^c_A (A)right) to THHleft(Mod^c_Aright) induced by the inclusion of A into Mod^c_A as a module over itself is an isomorphism. \label{ex:twist_thh_morita}
Let $A$ be a ring spectrum,  $Q$ be an $(A,A)$-bimodule, and  
\[
-\sma_AQ\colon  \operatorname{Mod}^c_A \to \operatorname{Mod}^c_A
\] 
be given by $M \mapsto M \sma_A Q$.  Then $(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}$ is 
an  $(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A, \operatorname{Mod}^c_A)$-bimodule and the inclusion 
\[
  E_A\colon  \End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A) \to \operatorname{Mod}^c_A
\] 
defines a $(\End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A),\End_{ \operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A))$-bimodule  $_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}$.  

Since $E_A$ is a Morita equivalence, applying \cref{cor:base_change_morita_isos} with the substitutions 
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c}
$\scr{A}$
&$\scr{C}$
&$F$
&$\scr{Q}$
\\
\hline
$\End_{\operatorname{Mod}^c_A}(A)$
&$\operatorname{Mod}^c_A$
&$E_A$
&$(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}$
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
gives an isomorphism $\sh{_{E_A}((\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ})_{E_A}} \to \sh{(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}}$. We also have identifications
  \begin{align*}
    & \sh{ {_{E_A}( (\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}})_{E_A}} = \sh{Q} = \operatorname{THH}(A; Q)\\
    &\sh{(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}} = \sh{(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A)_{-\sma_AQ}} = \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A ; {-\sma_AQ}) 
  \end{align*}

  \[
  \operatorname{THH}(A; Q)\to \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_A; {-\sma_AQ})
  \]
  Thus, the classical Morita invariance of $\operatorname{THH}$ holds in a twisted context as well.

We present two examples of these types of restriction-transfer identities
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $X$ be a path-connected space of  the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex. If we let $A=S$ and $C=\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X$, then $A$ is compact as a $C$-module.  The composite 
  \[
  S \simeq \operatorname{THH} (S) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}  \operatorname{THH} (\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{THH} (S) \simeq S 
  \]
is $\chi(X)$, regarded as an element of $\pi_0(S)$.
\item Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ where $[G:H] < \infty$.  Then the base change object associated to the inclusion of the group ring $A = \mathbb{Z}[H]$ into $C = \mathbb{Z}[G]$ is dualizable. The shadow is $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G])$ and 
  \[
  \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H],\mathbb{Z}[H]) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}   \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G],\mathbb{Z}[G]) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H], \mathbb{Z}[H]) 
  \]
  is multiplication by $[G:H]$. This has an interpretation in terms of the character theory of group representations, since $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G]) \cong \mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ where $C_G$ denotes the conjugacy classes of $G$. Since maps from $\mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ are exactly class functions, this is the same $[G:H]$ that appears in the classical induction-restriction maps in character theory for representations of finite groups.
\end{itemize}

Since traces are additive, the association $[f] \mapsto \operatorname{tr}(f)$ given by the composite \eqref{easy_trace} descends to a map from the Grothendieck group of endomorphisms of $A$-modules, also called $K_0 (\operatorname{End}(A))$. Thus, we obtain a map
  \[
  K_0 (\operatorname{End}(A)) \to \pi_0 \operatorname{THH}(A).
  \]
  Indeed, connoiseurs will recognize \eqref{easy_trace} as the usual ``inclusion of objects'' map that is used to define the cyclotomic trace (see, e.g. \cite{dundas_mccarthy}). We are only defining this at the level of $\pi_0$, so the usual difficulties don't intervene, but this is useful to keep in mind.

\label{ex_ab_group_base_change}
If $\scr{V}$ is the category of abelian groups and categories $\scr{C}$ and $\scr{D}$ each have  a single object, $\scr{C}$ is a ring $C$,  $\scr{D}$ is a ring $D$.  An $(\scr{C}, \scr{D}$)-bimodule $\scr{M}$ is an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$.  
If $i\colon \mathbb{Z}\to C$ is the map that picks out the monoidal unit, 
\[\rbm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iC}\to{_iC}\] is the ring multiplication in $C$ and 
\[\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iM}\to {_iM} \] is the module structure map.  

If $f\colon A\to C$ is a ring homomorphism, and $M$ is an $(C,D)$-bimodule 
\[\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{A}{A}{_fM}\colon _iA_i\otimes{ _i({_fM})}\to {_i({_fM})} \] 
is given by 
$\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{A}{A}{_fM}(a,m)=f(a)m$. 

\cref{prop:base_change_euler_monoid} implies the trace of the module structure map $\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}\colon _iC_i\otimes{ _iM}\to {_iM}$ is 
the composite 
\[\sh{_iC_i}\to \sh{C}\xrightarrow{\chi(M)} \sh{D}\]
The commuting diagram in \eqref{ex:connect_shadows_endo} identifies the first map as the map $C\to \sh{C}$.

If $\alpha \colon \bZ\to {_iC_i}$ is a module homomorphism,
the composite 
\[M\cong \bZ\otimes {_iM}\xrightarrow{\alpha\otimes \id} {_iC_i}\otimes {_iM} \xrightarrow{\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M}} {_iM}\] is given by $n\mapsto \alpha(1)n$.
While this is very similar to the description of $\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{A}{A}{_fM}$, since $\alpha$ is a module homomorphism there is greater flexibility in the image of $1$.

\cref{prop:base_change_euler_monoid} implies the trace of 
\[\mathbb{Z}\odot {_iM}\xrightarrow{\alpha \odot \id_{_iM}}{_iC_i}\odot {_iM}\xrightarrow{\rbmm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C}{M} } {_iM}\]
is $\sh{\mathbb{Z}}\xrightarrow{\sh{\alpha}} \sh{ _iC_i}\xrightarrow{\tr(\rbm{\epsilon}{i}{C}{C})}\sh{C}\xrightarrow{\chi(M)} \sh{D}$.

items.raw: As we will make clear, the natural home for $\operatorname{THH}$ is the bicategory of spectral categories. The other familiar property of $\operatorname{THH}$, Morita invariance, is a consequence of this structure. We emphasize that for proving general theorems about $\operatorname{THH}$ almost no other structure is used except for that provided by shadows. There is precedent for this viewpoint in the literature. In \cite{blumberg_mandell} the authors essentially manipulate $\operatorname{THH}$ as a shadow. As another example, in order to explore formal properties of Hochschild homology of DG-categories, Kaledin in \cite{kaledin} defines ``trace functors'' and then notes that they are similar to the second-named author's shadows. From this perspective, there is in some sense nothing ``special'' about $\operatorname{THH}$. Of course, its main property is that it receives a map from algebraic $K$-theory, but we are not yet using that structure.

Topological Hochschild homology is clearly functorial in the bimodule coordinate so that given a map of $(\scr{C}, \scr{C})$-bimodules $\scr{Q} \to \scr{Q}'$  there is a map
\[
\operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}; \scr{Q}) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}; \scr{Q}').  
\]
Furthermore, if $\scr{A} \to \scr{C}$ is a map, then we get an induced map $\operatorname{THH}(\scr{A}) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C})$. There is also a refinement of both \cite{blumberg_mandell}. Let $F\colon  \scr{A} \to \scr{C}$ be a map of spectral categories and let $\scr{Q}$ be a $(\scr{C},\scr{C})$-bimodule. Then there is a map
\[
\operatorname{THH}(\scr{A};{_F\scr{Q}_F}) \to \operatorname{THH}(\scr{C}, \scr{Q}) 
\]
and if there is a map $\scr{P} \to {_F \scr{Q}_F}$ we obtain
\[
\operatorname{THH}(\scr{A}; \scr{P}) \to \operatorname{THH} (\scr{C}, \scr{Q}). 
\]

items.raw: In the previous section, we showed that $\operatorname{THH}$ is an example of a shadow on a bicategory. This is quite a general notion, and many bicategories possess shadows. In addition, in any bicategory with shadow, one can define a notion of trace, which one can think of as a vast generalization of the trace of an endomorphism in a symmetric monoidal category. In this section we recall the definitions required to define a trace and collect the results about the trace that we will need below. It is at this point that we begin to work in bicategorical generality.

Given a map $f\colon  A \to C$ of monoids in a symmetric monoidal category $\scr{V}$, we can define an $(A, C)$-bimodule $ _f C$ which has an action on the left through $f\colon  A \to C$. Similarly, we get a $(C, A)$-bimodule $C_f$. These objects are used to \textit{change base} in the following sense. Given a $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$, computing the composition $_f C\odot  M$ is the same as computing $(f\times \id_D)^\ast M$. 
These types of objects arise in any bicategory defined from an indexed monoidal category \cite{ps:indexed}, but we need not work in that generality here. Instead, we work in the two examples from \cref{sect:duality_and_trace}.

Let $R$ be a ring spectrum and $A$, $C$ be $R$-algebras.  A map of $R$-algebras $f\colon  A \to C$ defines an $(A, C)$-bimodule $_fC$.  If 
$_fC$

an adjunction
\[
 C_f \sma_A - \colon  \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(A, R)} \leftrightarrows \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(C, R)} \colon  \ _f C \sma_C - 
\]
between the bimodules that are left-compact (that is, for example, an $(A, R)$-bimodule is compact when considered as an $A$-module). Letting $R$ be the sphere spectrum and taking $\operatorname{THH}$ of both sides of the adjunction gives us maps
\[
\operatorname{res}\colon  \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{A}) \leftrightarrows \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_C) \colon  \operatorname{trf} 
\]
which are usually referred to as \textbf{restriction} and \textbf{transfer}. There is a restriction for any map $f$, but there is only a transfer if 
$C$ is compact as an $A$-module. Using Morita invariance 
restriction and transfer  give maps between $\operatorname{THH}(A)$ and $\operatorname{THH}(C)$. 
We should note that the transfer map has appeared in many $\operatorname{THH}$ calculations and seems to provide powerful characteristic-type invariants \cite{schlichtkrull_1, schlichtkrull_2, bentzen_madsen}.

It is well know that the composite
\[
S \cong \operatorname{THH}(S) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{trf}} \operatorname{THH}(\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} }  \operatorname{THH} (S) \simeq S 
\]
is the Euler characteristic.  In this section we show that similar results hold for the generalizations of the Euler characteristics used in fixed point theory.

full.raw: As we will make clear, the natural home for $\operatorname{THH}$ is the bicategory of spectral categories. The other familiar property of $\operatorname{THH}$, Morita invariance, is a consequence of this structure. We emphasize that for proving general theorems about $\operatorname{THH}$ almost no other structure is used except for that provided by shadows. There is precedent for this viewpoint in the literature. In \cite{blumberg_mandell} the authors essentially manipulate $\operatorname{THH}$ as a shadow. As another example, in order to explore formal properties of Hochschild homology of DG-categories, Kaledin in \cite{kaledin} defines ``trace functors'' and then notes that they are similar to the second-named author's shadows. From this perspective, there is in some sense nothing ``special'' about $\operatorname{THH}$. Of course, its main property is that it receives a map from algebraic $K$-theory, but we are not yet using that structure.

full.raw: In the previous section, we showed that $\operatorname{THH}$ is an example of a shadow on a bicategory. This is quite a general notion, and many bicategories possess shadows. In addition, in any bicategory with shadow, one can define a notion of trace, which one can think of as a vast generalization of the trace of an endomorphism in a symmetric monoidal category. In this section we recall the definitions required to define a trace and collect the results about the trace that we will need below. It is at this point that we begin to work in bicategorical generality.

For rings $C$ and $D$, an $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ is right dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a right $D$-module.  
A choice of dual is the $(D,C)$-bimodule of right $D$-module homomorphisms $\Hom_D(M,D)$.  Note that $\Hom_D(M,D)$ is regarded as a $(D,C)$-bimodule using the left $C$-module structure on $M$ and left $D$-module structure on $D$. 

The coevaluation map is the composite  
\[
  C\to \Hom_D(M,M)\xleftarrow{\sim} M\otimes_D\Hom_D(M,D)
\] 
where
the second map is an isomorphism since $M$ is  finitely generated and projective as an $D$ module. 
The evaluation map for this dual pair is the  evaluation map 
\[
  \Hom_D(M,D)\otimes_C M\to D.
\]

Dually, $M$ is left dualizable if it is finitely generated and projective as a left $C$-module.

In the bicategory of rings, bimodules, and homomorphisms, a Morita equivalence is a $(C,D)$-bimodule $M$ and a $(D,C)$-bimodule $N$ so that  $(M,N)$ and $(N,M)$ are dual pairs and, using the coevaluation and evaluation from these dual pairs, 
 \[
  M\otimes_DN\cong C\qquad\text{and} \qquad N\otimes_CM\cong D.
 \]
This is the familiar notion of Morita equivalence for rings and implies the  functor 
\[
 N\otimes_C- \colon \Mod_C\to \Mod_D
\] 
is equivalence of the category of (left) modules over $C$ and the category of (left) modules over $D$. 

The most familiar example of Morita equivalence is that the ring of $n$-by-$n$ matrices with elements in $C$ is Morita equivalent to $C$ for any $n > 0$.

Let $R$ be a ring spectrum and $A$, $C$ be $R$-algebras.  A map of $R$-algebras $f\colon  A \to C$ defines an $(A, C)$-bimodule $_fC$.  If 
$_fC$
 is left dualizable, we have 
an adjunction
\[
 C_f \sma_A - \colon  \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(A, R)} \leftrightarrows \operatorname{Mod}^{lc}_{(C, R)} \colon  \ _f C \sma_C - 
\]
between the bimodules that are left-compact (that is, for example, an $(A, R)$-bimodule is compact when considered as an $A$-module). Letting $R$ be the sphere spectrum and taking $\operatorname{THH}$ of both sides of the adjunction gives us maps
\[
\operatorname{res}\colon  \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_{A}) \leftrightarrows \operatorname{THH}(\operatorname{Mod}^c_C) \colon  \operatorname{trf} 
\]
which are usually referred to as \textbf{restriction} and \textbf{transfer}. There is a restriction for any map $f$, but there is only a transfer if 
$C$ is compact as an $A$-module. Using Morita invariance 
restriction and transfer  give maps between $\operatorname{THH}(A)$ and $\operatorname{THH}(C)$. 
We should note that the transfer map has appeared in many $\operatorname{THH}$ calculations and seems to provide powerful characteristic-type invariants \cite{schlichtkrull_1, schlichtkrull_2, bentzen_madsen}.

It is well know that the composite
\[
S \cong \operatorname{THH}(S) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{trf}} \operatorname{THH}(\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} }  \operatorname{THH} (S) \simeq S 
\]
is the Euler characteristic.  In this section we show that similar results hold for the generalizations of the Euler characteristics used in fixed point theory.
In particular we show that the spectrum-level Reidemeister trace of the second author \cite{p:thesis,p:coincidence} arises from transfer maps in $\operatorname{THH}$. The transfer maps we use are ``twisted'' by a bimodule coordinate in $\operatorname{THH}$.

We present two examples of these types of restriction-transfer identities
\begin{itemize}
\item Let $X$ be a path-connected space of  the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex. If we let $A=S$ and $C=\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X$, then $A$ is compact as a $C$-module.  The composite 
  \[
  S \simeq \operatorname{THH} (S) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}  \operatorname{THH} (\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega X) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{THH} (S) \simeq S 
  \]
is $\chi(X)$, regarded as an element of $\pi_0(S)$.
\item Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ where $[G:H] < \infty$.  Then the base change object associated to the inclusion of the group ring $A = \mathbb{Z}[H]$ into $C = \mathbb{Z}[G]$ is dualizable. The shadow is $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G])$ and 
  \[
  \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H],\mathbb{Z}[H]) \xrightarrow{ \operatorname{trf}}   \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G],\mathbb{Z}[G]) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{res} } \operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[H], \mathbb{Z}[H]) 
  \]
  is multiplication by $[G:H]$. This has an interpretation in terms of the character theory of group representations, since $\operatorname{HH}_0 (\mathbb{Z}[G], \mathbb{Z}[G]) \cong \mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ where $C_G$ denotes the conjugacy classes of $G$. Since maps from $\mathbb{Z}[C_G]$ are exactly class functions, this is the same $[G:H]$ that appears in the classical induction-restriction maps in character theory for representations of finite groups.
\end{itemize}

We consider the case when $n = 2$ for the map $B$ above, which is enough to capture the issues. We define
  \[
  \widetilde{\omega} = \omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)
  \]
  and  a family of paths parameterized by the 2-simplex \[\Delta^2 = \{(u_0, u_1, u_2) : u_0 + u_1 + u_2 = 1\}.\] 
We think of this simplex as interpolating between three extremes: the cases when each of $u_0, u_1$ and $u_2$ are 1. We'd like the extreme cases to be
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $u_2 = 1$ --- the path $\omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega$
  \item $u_1 = 1$ --- the path $\omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0)$
  \item $u_0 = 1$ --- the path $\omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)$. 
  \end{itemize}
  We would also like that if the path starts at $x$, the endpoint is $f(x)$. Consider the path 
  \begin{align*}
    \widetilde{\omega} (t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1| + |\omega|) + u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|))
  \end{align*}
  We can check that when $u_2 = 1$ then $u_0, u_1 = 0$ and the above gives $\widetilde{\omega}(t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|+|\omega|))$ which is exactly $\omega_0 \ast \omega_1 \ast \omega$. When $u_1 = 1$, then the above is $\widetilde{\omega}(t(|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + |\omega_0|)$, which is the path $\omega_1 \ast \omega \ast f(\omega_0)$. Finally, when $u_0 = 1$ we get the path $\omega \ast f(\omega_0) \ast f(\omega_1)$.

  We also note that for any choice of $u_0, u_1$, 
  \begin{align*}
    &\widetilde{\omega}(u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|)\\
    &= \widetilde{\omega} (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1| + |\omega| + u_0 (|\omega_0| + |\omega_1|) + u_1 (|\omega_0|))
  \end{align*}
  essentially by definition, so that each path parameterized by $u_0, u_1, u_2$ is in $\scr{L} X^f$.

full.raw: The space $\scr{L} X^f$ is the space of homotopy fixed points of a self-map $f\colon  X \to X$, computed by taking a ``derived intersection'' of $X$ and the image of $X$ under $f$. One could wish to have a similar $\operatorname{THH}$ description of the derived intersection of two maps $f, g\colon  X \to Y$. The following corollary is a more general statement, and easy corollary of the proof of \cref{main_geometric_theorem}. Though we do not use this generality in the paper, it is useful to record for later work.
